name: Unfalsifiable Timelines
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: A Prediction You Can Never Prove Wrong
lesson.summary: Some quantum computing timelines are constructed so vaguely that no future outcome could ever contradict them, a trap that forms when the 3-5 Years Away Pattern combines with the Moving Goalposts Pattern to produce a claim that resists all evidence.
lesson.body:
A good prediction is falsifiable, meaning it specifies, in advance, some observation that would prove it wrong. "It will rain in this city sometime in the next decade" is technically a prediction, but it is nearly useless, because almost any decade in almost any city includes rain. "It will rain here tomorrow at 3pm" is a real prediction, because a dry afternoon would clearly refute it. The philosopher Karl Popper argued that this property, falsifiability, is what separates a scientific claim from one that merely sounds scientific. A claim that cannot be shown wrong by any possible observation is not really telling you anything about the world.

Some of the boldest quantum computing predictions fail this test not because they are stated vaguely on purpose, but because the 3-5 Years Away Pattern and the Moving Goalposts Pattern combine to make them vague in practice, even when the original wording sounded precise. "Practical, world changing quantum computers are three to five years away" sounds like a real prediction, with a real deadline. But "practical" and "world changing" are never pinned down to a specific, measurable benchmark, so when the deadline passes, there is no agreed upon test the claim has failed. Was a quantum computer that beat a classical computer at one contrived, unused benchmark task "practical"? Reasonable people can argue endlessly, and that endless argument is exactly the point: it lets the original prediction survive contact with reality by hiding behind ambiguity.

Combine this with moving goalposts and you get a genuinely unfalsifiable claim: any evidence that seems to refute the prediction gets absorbed by quietly redefining what the prediction meant, and any evidence that seems to support it gets celebrated without a matching willingness to have been proven wrong if it had not shown up. A claim that responds to disconfirming evidence by simply changing its own meaning is not a scientific prediction anymore, no matter how technical it sounds or how credentialed the person making it is. It functions more like an article of faith, always renewed, never tested.

This does not mean every long range quantum computing claim is worthless, and it does not mean skepticism should collapse into the position that nothing can ever be predicted. Plenty of quantum computing predictions are perfectly falsifiable: a specific qubit count by a specific year, a specific error rate on a specific hardware platform, a named algorithm demonstrated on a named problem size. Those are testable, and the field should be judged by how well they hold up. The unfalsifiable ones are the ones worth flagging loudly, because they are structured to survive no matter what happens, which means they cannot actually be evidence for anything.

A simple test to apply when you hear a big quantum computing claim: ask what specific, observable outcome, by what specific date, would count as this prediction having failed. If the person making the claim cannot answer that question, or answers it in terms so soft that almost any outcome could be squeezed into a win, you are listening to an unfalsifiable timeline, not a scientific forecast. That distinction sets up the next chapter, which looks at the companion trick of quietly redefining what success means after a deadline has already passed rather than before it.
